produced_by: meaning-review workflow (classifier per rule group + adversarial refuter per SAFE verdict), 2026-09-25
standard: SAFE only if the auto-fix never changes what a paper says and every change is what a careful author would want; one measured meaning-changing or wrong-for-context case makes a rule UNSAFE (OPEN-112).

MATH-046.what_the_fix_does: Finds every `,[ ]*\ldots[ ]*,` match inside math (validators_l1_math.ml:2046-2114) and replaces `\ldots` with `\cdots` byte for byte (6 bytes to 6 bytes). The result is that every comma-separated list ellipsis `x_1, \ldots, x_n` becomes `x_1, \cdots, x_n`, so the PDF shows centred dots `· · ·` where it showed baseline dots `. . .`.
MATH-046.examples: All 5 cases (every one compiles, rc 0/0). 2507.11254v1 (171 edits): `{1, 2, . . . , n}` -> `{1, 2, · · · , n}` and `[v1 , v2 , . . . , vn ]` -> `[v1 , v2 , · · · , vn ]`. 2506.13950v1 (100 edits): the superscript index `\alpha_n^{i_1,\ldots,i_M}` -> `αni1 ,··· ,iM`, and `for q=1,\ldots,Q`. 2507.10327v1 (59 edits): `vec(A) = (a1,1 , . . . , an,1 , ...)` -> centred dots, plus the multinomial `{k\choose a_1,\ldots,a_n}`; the page count went 15 -> 16. 2506.09151v1 (73 edits): `|e1⟩, |e2⟩, . . . , |e2d⟩` -> `· · ·` and `{1, . . . , d}`; the page count went 92 -> 93. 2507.11295v1 (93 edits, unicode-math): `[0; j1 , . . . , jn ]` -> `[0; j1 , ⋯, jn ]`.
MATH-046.rationale:
MEASURED: I copied all 5 audit papers into scratchpad/math046, ran the fixer with LP_FIX_ONLY=MATH-046 and LP_FIX_TRACE, and got 496 applied edits (73/100/59/171/93). Every one of the 496 is exactly `\ldots` -> `\cdots` with a comma on both sides, in math. I checked the offset count against the trace count for each file. Output length is unchanged, so the rule makes no other kind of source edit. I also read all 125 PDF word hunks the JSON records (of 851 in total). Every hunk that touches the ellipsis is `. . .` -> `· · ·` or `⋯` between commas.

Why every edit is wrong for its context: the standard convention says the opposite of what the rule assumes. The TeXbook (ch. 18) and amsmath's `\dotsc` (dots between commas) both say to use baseline dots in a comma list and centred dots only between binary operators or relations, as in `a_1 + \cdots + a_n`. The rule's premise, `\ldots` 'on relation axis; prefer \cdots between commas', has that backwards. It rewrites every correctly typeset list, set, tuple and index sequence into the non-standard form, including cases where the typeset result is plainly worse: `αni1 ,··· ,iM`, `{1, · · · , d}`, and a multinomial `\choose` argument. A careful author would want none of these. No meaning changed: the symbols, words and mathematics are the same, and the dots still read as an ellipsis. So the count is 0 meaning-changing and 496 of 496 wrong for context.

INFERRED, not rebuilt: the remaining PDF hunks look like reordering or dropped tokens, for example `xS`/`⊤` moving in 2506.13950v1, display equations reshuffled in 2507.10327v1 and 2506.09151v1, page-number tokens moving, and `(x)−w(x)` -> `(x) − w(x)` in 2507.11295v1. I did not rebuild to confirm them. They are pdftotext extraction artefacts of reflow, not content changes: the source edits are fully enumerated and are only the 496 dot swaps, and the `−w(x)` line (MultidimCLT.tex:373) contains no MATH-046 edit.

Verdict: UNSAFE. The 'fix' is a wrong typographic rewrite applied to 100% of its sites. It also pushed a page break in 2 of 5 papers. The rule's detector premise (flagging `,\ldots,`) should itself be reconsidered, not only its fix.

STYLE-033.what_the_fix_does: Deletes the single space byte before every ` \cite` that is not preceded by `~` (latex-parse/src/validators_l4_style.ml, r_style_033: Cst_edit.delete pos..pos+1). It does not insert a tie. The rule's own message says 'use ~ (non-breaking space)', but the fix removes the interword space altogether, so 'in \cite{x}' becomes 'in\cite{x}' and prints as 'in[x]'. The unit test in test_validators_style.ml pins this output ('As shown\cite{smith2020}').
STYLE-033.examples: 2506.17123v1: 'third author and M. Cabanes [CS24])' -> 'M. Cabanes[CS24])'; 'see [Sp09, 4.1] and [Sp10, 4.3]' -> 'see[Sp09, 4.1] and[Sp10, 4.3]'. 2507.08439v1: 'see e.g. [5–11].' -> 'see e.g.[5– 11].', so the citation range now breaks across a line because the break point before the bracket is gone. 2507.05614v1: 'for example, [8] and' -> 'for example,[8] and' (source edit at byte 10679, 'for example, \cite{kaji15}', traced via LP_FIX_TRACE).
STYLE-033.rationale: MEASURED: I rebuilt all 3 audit cases (pristine and LP_FIX_ONLY=STYLE-033), pdflatex rc 0/0 each, with the full uncapped word diff: 2 + 46 + 162 = 210 hunks. The trace logged 2 + 42 + 151 = 195 edits, and every edit is a 1-byte delete with an empty replacement. Of the 210 hunks, 178 glue the preceding word or punctuation directly onto the citation bracket ('in[NSV20]', 'Cabanes[CS24]', 'e.g.[5–11]', 'example,[8]'). That is the wrong fix in every context: the correct typography is 'in~[NSV20]', which keeps the space and forbids the break, and this output is worse than the input. The other 32 hunks are line-reflow side effects: moved or reordered tokens, new hyphenation such as 'mod- ify', and a footnote shifting position. I checked this with a multiset comparison of tokens. After splitting at '[' and ignoring hyphens and whitespace, the only differences are word fragments that line breaks split or rejoined. No words, symbols or maths were added or lost, so no hunk changes meaning. INFERRED: the defect is systematic, not a matter of sampling. The fix deletes the space unconditionally, so every edit on every paper produces 'word[cite]'. With natbib author-year styles this would glue text onto '(Author, year)' too, but that case is not in the sample. The correct fix already exists as TYPO-016's tie insertion. STYLE-033's fix should be withdrawn or replaced by '~' rather than allow-listed.

SCRIPT-007.what_the_fix_does: Inside math, rewrites every subscript `_{X}` to `_{\text{X}}` when X is 3 or more ASCII letters, X is not on a 19-word operator list, and none of `\text{`/`\mathrm{`/`\operatorname{` appears in the 16 bytes before it (latex-parse/src/validators_l1.ml:1425-1547). It never checks whether X is a word label or a list of index or derivative letters.
SCRIPT-007.examples: MEASURED, outside the 5 sampled papers (fixer run with LP_FIX_ONLY=SCRIPT-007 on corpus copies; all exited 0). (1) 2506.13645v1 StokesFDM2025June16.tex: `u^{(1)}_{xxx}` -> `u^{(1)}_{\text{xxx}}` and `u^{(2)}_{xxy}` -> `_{\text{xxy}}`, 15 of 17 wrapped. These are third partial derivatives, which should stay in math italic, and the neighbouring `\phi_{xx}` stays italic. (2) 2507.04261v1 Manuscript.tex: `f_{ttt}+f_{uuu}f^3` -> `f_{\text{ttt}}+f_{\text{uuu}}f^3`, while `f_{tt}f_u` and `f_{tu}` stay math. (3) 2506.14455v1 nry_unified.tex: `u_{ttt}(0)` -> `u_{\text{ttt}}(0)` 28 of 54 times, next to untouched `u_t`, `\theta_{tt}`, `p_{tt}`. (4) 2507.09229v1: the tensor index `\tilde{h}_{ijkl}` -> `\tilde{h}_{\text{ijkl}}` (3 of 3), next to `t_{ij}`. MEASURED in the sample, by source edit plus TeX's known behaviour: (5) 2506.20048v1 draft_current.tex:1575, inside `\begin{corollary}` (plain theorem style, italic body): `\MMD_{cou}^2` -> `\MMD_{\text{cou}}^2`. `\text` takes the surrounding italic font, so the 4 corollary occurrences come out italic while the other 38 (for example `k_{\text{cou}}` on p.24) come out upright. One symbol, two typefaces.
SCRIPT-007.rationale: MEASURED, 5 sampled papers (trace-matched, 299 edits; word_hunks_total 0+16+46+34+82=178). I reviewed every source edit, not just the 25 hunks per case in the audit file. The labels wrapped were cou, divide, SNS, LNS, intra, Rem, Both, tot, wait, mono, mseclr, anc, nceclr, ddpm, neg, bal, tail, unc, cond, uncond, pos, category, frac, LSR, main. All are descriptive labels where an upright subscript is correct. So 144 PDF hunks are intended (math-italic 'bSN S' becomes upright 'bSNS', and 'D f rac' becomes 'Dfrac'). The 34 odd-looking hunks in 2507.09052v1 (for example 'hianc · hjneg' -> 'hi · hjneg' and 'πancπanc+πneg' -> 'πancπ+π ) neg') are only pdftotext reading-order changes. I rebuilt the paper and rendered pages 5 and 6: the displays are unchanged apart from the upright subscripts, and eq. (1) no longer runs into the margin. No sampled hunk changes what the paper says. The rule is still UNSAFE, for two reasons. (a) The predicate cannot tell a word label from a string of index or derivative letters. A grep of the corpus finds `_{ijk}` 314 times, `_{ijkl}` 83, `_{ttt}` 78, `_{uuu}` 39, `_{xxx}` 36, `_{uuv}` 32 and `_{uvr}` 33. Probes of 4 papers (MEASURED) show the fixer turning partial-derivative subscripts and tensor indices into upright text, 55 wrong edits in all. The result is also inconsistent within the same formula (`f_{\text{ttt}}` next to `f_{tt}`). A careful author would never want this. Not every such subscript is wrapped: `\epsilon_{ijk}` in 2507.08763v1 was left alone (0 of 2), for reasons I did not trace. (b) In the sample itself, `\text{}` inherits the text font, so in an italic theorem body the 'fix' gives an italic subscript that differs from the same symbol elsewhere (4 edits in 2506.20048v1). That is wrong for its context. The 4 are MEASURED at the source level; the italic rendering is INFERRED from how `\text` works, because I could not isolate the corollary glyphs in the crop. Also INFERRED, not measured: `\text` needs amsmath, so a paper without it would fail to compile. That would be a break, not a change of meaning. The counts in the numeric fields: intended_typography=144 of the 178 in-sample PDF hunks, and the other 34 are extraction-order artifacts that are neither intended nor harmful. wrong_for_context=59 is 4 in-sample edits plus 55 out-of-sample probe edits; those are source edits, not PDF hunks. One wrong-for-context case is enough to make a rule unsafe, and there are 59.

SCRIPT-005.what_the_fix_does: Inside math, rewrites a superscript `^l` (l not followed by an alphanumeric) to `^{\ell}`, and `^{l}` to `^{\ell}` (validators_l1.ml ~1300-1384). It changes only the superscript occurrence. It never checks whether the same `l` is used elsewhere as a summation index, subscript or prose variable.
SCRIPT-005.examples: 2506.14893v1: `\sum_{l=0}^t\alpha_{ijkl}X^iY^j\otimes S^kT^{l}` -> `...S^kT^{\ell}`. The bound index stays `l=0`, but the exponent is now ℓ. The same file also has `(T-m)^{\ell}=\sum_{l=0}^tm^lv_l`, where `m^l` stays l, and `T^{l+1}` stays l beside `T^{\ell}`. PDF: 'S k T l , i=0 j=0 k=0 l=0' -> 'S k T ℓ , ... l=0'. | 2507.11418v1: `\sum_{l=0}^{L_2}\sum_{j=0}^{\ell} a_{j,l} \frac{x^{\ell}}{M^{5l-2j}}`. One variable is now spelled ℓ in the limit and exponent but l in the index, subscript and M^{5l-2j}. | 2507.09627v1: `C^{in}_l = 2^{\ell} C_0^{out}` and `\sum_{l=0}^{L-1} \frac{H_0W_0}{4^{\ell}}`. | 2507.09242v1: `O_{se}^{\ell}` 'represents the output ... at layer \( l \)' and `\sum_{l=1}^{L}\alpha_l L_{style}^{\ell}`. | 2506.20048v1: `\nqextensionsurrogate^{\ell}` 'for some $l\geq 2$' and `2^{l(j-1)}\cdot\deltan^{\ell}`.
SCRIPT-005.rationale: MEASURED. I found 5 cases in meaning.json, with 140 word hunks in total. I reviewed all word hunks listed in the data (the first 25 per case, 106 in all). I then rebuilt all 5 cases with LP_FIX_ONLY=SCRIPT-005 and LP_FIX_TRACE, which logged 87 source edits (79 `{\ell}`, 8 `\ell`), and read the full source diffs. That covers every edit, including those behind the hunks beyond 25. In every one of the 5 papers the rewritten `l` is a variable that the same formula, or the surrounding prose, still writes as plain `l`: sum indices, subscripts like a_{j,l}, W_l and alpha_l, exponents like 5l-2j and l+1, and 'layer \( l \)' / 'for some $l\geq 2$'. So the fix splits one variable into two different glyphs. A reader sees ℓ and l as distinct symbols, and the mathematics no longer says what the author wrote. None of the 5 source files used \ell anywhere before the fix (grep count 0 in 2506.14893v1; the other files show no pre-existing \ell in the changed lines). No hunk qualifies as intended typography, because a careful author changes l to ℓ everywhere or nowhere. Hunk split, INFERRED from the first-25 lists: about 58 glyph-substitution hunks are meaning-changing. About 24 hunks are pdftotext reading-order shuffles caused by the width change; these are mostly in 2507.11418v1 (equation blocks re-ordered), plus 2 each in 2507.09242v1 and 2507.09627v1. I recorded those as wrong-for-context layout side effects, not as further meaning changes. Measured source edits: 87/87 sit next to a live plain-`l` use of the same variable in the same paper, as read in the diffs; this was not checked by an automated per-edit test. The rebuild directories and traces are in scratchpad/script/.

SCRIPT-001.what_the_fix_does: Inside math, wraps a bare all-digit multi-character subscript `_12...` in braces as `_{12...}` (OPEN-070 narrowed it to all-digit runs, validators_l1.ml 954-1050). The code comment assumes `x_12` must mean a two-digit subscript because 'nobody writes x_1 next to a bare 2'.
SCRIPT-001.examples: 2506.14940v1 (the only case): `$\om\in\{(a_10000),(a_11000),(a_10001),(a_10100)\}$` -> `(a_{10000}),(a_{11000}),(a_{10001}),(a_{10100})`. PDF: '(a1 0000)' -> '(a10000 )'. These are highest-weight coordinate vectors whose first coordinate is a_1 and the rest are 0/1 digits. The source proves the reading: `\om=(a_10001)= a\om_1+\om_5`, and the author elsewhere writes `(a_1 10000)` with an explicit space. After the fix one line reads `(a_{100000}),(a_1 10000),(a_{100001})`, so the three vectors are now typeset inconsistently. Every other hunk has the same shape: `(a_100000)` -> `(a_{100000})` and `(a_100001)` -> `(a_{100001})`, 12 source edits in total.
SCRIPT-001.rationale: MEASURED. There is 1 case (2506.14940v1), with 9 word hunks, all reviewed, and 12 source edits, confirmed by rebuilding with LP_FIX_ONLY=SCRIPT-001 and LP_FIX_TRACE. All 9 hunks change the mathematics. The author wrote a_1 followed by digit coordinates, and TeX rendered exactly that. The fix turns it into a variable a indexed by 10000, 10001 and so on, which contradicts the paper's own identity (a_10001) = aω_1 + ω_5. This real paper refutes the premise in the rule's code comment ('nobody writes x_1 next to a bare 2'): writing weight or Dynkin-label vectors as a_1 followed by digits is exactly that pattern. The digit-only narrowing from OPEN-070 removed the fatal Double-subscript breaks, but not the silent meaning change. The evidence is a single paper, but a clean compile makes the damage invisible, and every sampled hunk was wrong (9/9). Rebuild artefacts are in scratchpad/script/2506.14940v1.{diff,trace}.

TYPO-032.what_the_fix_does: Deletes the comma in any `,[ ]*\cite` match. Because it is a prefix match, this covers \cite, \citep, \citet, \citealt and \citealp. It skips `\,` and exempt regions. Source: latex-parse/src/validators_l0_typo.ml:1497-1545.
TYPO-032.examples: MEASURED. I rebuilt all 5 cases in full: 101 word hunks, 75 source edits in the trace. After normalising whitespace and hyphens, the only characters that differ between the pristine and fixed PDFs are commas: 11+13+19+23+9 = 75 commas removed and nothing added. The other 26 hunks are reflow. Of the 75 deletions, 25 are separators between two citations and 50 follow introductory or parenthetical phrases. None of the 75 is a case where the comma was wrong. (1) 2507.10380v1: '(Crapsi et al. 2007, Navarro-Almaida et al. 2023, Esplugues et al. 2022, ...)' -> '(Crapsi et al. 2007 Navarro-Almaida et al. 2023 Esplugues et al. 2022 ...)'. The citation list runs together. (2) 2507.07350v1: 'for example, [MP25], [FL24], [FL24b], ...' -> 'for example [MP25] [FL24] [FL24b] ...'. (3) 2507.10834v1: 'For instance, Bront et al. (2009) show' -> 'For instance Bront et al. (2009) show', plus 16 more of this kind ('Furthermore,', 'Similarly,', 'First,', 'Second,'). (4) 2507.09936v1: '(e.g., McKee & Tan 2003)' -> '(e.g. McKee & Tan 2003)' and '(AMR, Berger & Oliger 1984)' -> '(AMR Berger & Oliger 1984)'. (5) 2507.11154v1: '(e.g., [5, Theorem 1.5.11], [7, Theorem 2.45])' -> '(e.g. [5, Theorem 1.5.11] [7, Theorem 2.45])'.
TYPO-032.rationale: MEASURED. In every paper and every edit, the fix deletes punctuation that is grammatically required. With author-year citations, which is every astro and OR paper sampled, this merges the items of a citation list. The rule's premise, that a comma before \cite is an anti-pattern, is false for \citet/\citealt/\citealp and for lists of \cite. 0 of 75 edits were improvements.

TYPO-003.what_the_fix_does: Replaces every `---` outside exempt regions (verbatim, comments, math, url) with a UTF-8 em-dash U+2014. It has no context guard for \texttt or {\tt}. Source: validators_l0_typo.ml:246-274.
TYPO-003.examples: MEASURED in the sample: 5 papers, 88 source edits. All are prose em-dashes, including affiliations like 'Technion---Israel', 'Introduction.---' run-in heads and '&---' table placeholders. In all 5 the PDF character multiset is identical to pristine, ignoring whitespace and hyphens. The 31 hunks are reflow only. For example, 2507.01430v1 'predictors— which' -> 'predictors—which': the pristine PDF broke the line after the dash, and the Unicode dash (\textemdash) is no longer a break point. 2507.10415v1 has 29 reflow hunks for the same reason. MEASURED out of sample, 1 wrong-for-context: 2507.06726v1 has a ruler of hyphens in R console output, '\texttt{----...----}' (52 hyphens). The fix turns it into '—————————————————' (17 em-dashes), where pristine rendered 26 '–'. The printed code output changes. CONSTRUCTED probe (default OT1, no fontenc): '\texttt{a---b}' renders as 'a---b' pristine and as 'a|b' after the fix, a garbled glyph.
TYPO-003.rationale: The sample is clean: every edit is a genuine em-dash, and the PDF text is unchanged apart from lost break opportunities after the dash. But in a real corpus paper the fix rewrites a monospace or code context where `---` means three literal hyphens (2507.06726v1). In OT1 typewriter the result is a wrong glyph ('|'). Under pdflatex the fix gives no textual benefit, since `---` already typesets an em-dash. It could become safe only with a guard for \texttt and {\tt}.

TYPO-004.what_the_fix_does: Replaces `` with U+201C and '' with U+201D outside exempt regions. It does not check the font or typewriter context. Source: validators_l0_typo.ml:276-331.
TYPO-004.examples: MEASURED: 5 papers, 200 source edits. 2 papers (2507.03884v1, 2507.09209v1) had 0 edits when the rule ran alone. Every edit is a correctly paired quotation, for example 2506.20779v1 ``neural shattering'' -> “neural shattering”, and the IEEE bibliography titles in 2506.21499v1. The PDF character multiset is identical in all 3 papers with edits. The only word hunks are 12 in 2507.09513v1, all table and float reflow ('fine- tuned' moving around a table). MEASURED out of sample: 2507.08396v1, with \texttt{``fairy''} under T1, had 14 edits and 0 text change. Non-UTF-8-inputenc papers (2507.04257v1, 2507.08692v1) and 2507.10873v1 got 0 edits, so the fixer appears to guard them. CONSTRUCTED probe (article class, no fontenc, i.e. OT1): 'C \texttt{``c''}' renders 'C ‘‘c’’' pristine and 'C \c"' after the fix. The OT1 typewriter font maps \textquotedblleft and \textquotedblright to the backslash and straight-quote slots.
TYPO-004.rationale: No bad hunk was measured: all 200 sampled edits are intended quotation marks, and the PDF text is character-identical, so the fix has zero visible benefit under pdflatex. However, a reproducible failure turns quotes inside \texttt under the default OT1 encoding into '\c"' garbage. The corpus contains \texttt{``...''} (2507.08396v1, 2507.10873v1, 2507.09949v1), though the OT1 combination was not observed to fire. The instruction is 'when in doubt: unsafe' and withholding costs nothing, so I call it UNSAFE. That rests on INFERRED risk, not on a measured corpus hunk. A guard for \texttt and {\tt} would likely make it safe.

TYPO-034.what_the_fix_does: Deletes the space in every ` \footnote` substring outside exempt regions. It is a raw PREFIX match, so it also fires on ` \footnotesize`, ` \footnotemark` and ` \footnotetext`. Source: validators_l0_typo.ml:1609-1641.
TYPO-034.examples: MEASURED in the sample: 4 papers with edits (2507.07721v1 had 0). 2507.04739v1: 5 real footnotes in \author, 'Lorenzo Anoè ∗' -> 'Lorenzo Anoè∗', which is intended. 2507.09183v1, 2507.09217v1 and 2507.09513v1: every edit hit an indented '    \footnotesize' at the start of a line. These are misfires on the wrong macro, harmless there because the newline still supplies a space, and produce 0 PDF change. MEASURED out of sample, meaning-changing: 2507.11506v1/eval.tex:477 '\caption{Interconnect utilization at varied \footnotesize HBM \small bandwidths.}' -> 'varied\footnotesize HBM'. After a full rebuild (rc 0 both) the PDF reads 'Figure 21: Interconnect utilization at variedHBM bandwidths.' instead of 'varied HBM bandwidths.' CONSTRUCTED probe confirms the same: 'print \footnotesize below' -> 'printbelow'.
TYPO-034.rationale: Its prefix match treats \footnotesize as \footnote. In a real corpus paper the fix fuses two words in a figure caption (rc 0, a silent meaning change). In the sample, most of its edits target \footnotesize rather than a footnote. The genuine footnote edits are fine, but one corrupting case is disqualifying. It would need a word-boundary check after '\footnote' (not followed by a letter).

TYPO-016.what_the_fix_does: Replaces the single space byte immediately before `\cite` or `\ref` (regex ` \\(cite|ref)[^a-zA-Z]`) with `~`, unless that byte is in the exempt set (verbatim, comment, url, math). It does not look at what comes before the space. Source: latex-parse/src/validators_l0_typo.ml:829-869.
TYPO-016.examples: (1) 2507.09737v1 Seneta-Heyde_BRW52.tex, `Under conditions  \ref{...}` becomes `Under conditions  ~\ref{...}`. The source has two spaces, the rule replaces the second, so the output is a space followed by a tie: a visible double gap. `x  ~\ref` measured 22.80pt against 19.47pt for `x \ref`, which is +3.33pt. Other instances: `(cf.\  \cite` becomes `(cf.\ ~\cite` (27.80pt vs 24.47pt), and `or  \cite` becomes `or  ~\cite`. (2) 2506.09151v1 introduction.tex, `Appendix \n    \ref{sec:circuit_compilation}` becomes `Appendix \n   ~\ref{...}`. The end-of-line space plus the tie gives a double space (measured 22.80pt), and the tie does not stop the break because the earlier space can still break. (3) 2506.20910v1 arxiv_v1_main.tex has 7 of these: `...classes of MDPs. \cite{fruit_efficient_2018, ...}` becomes `MDPs.~\cite{...}`, and `\citep{sabach_first_2017}. \cite{lieder...} and` changes the same way. Here the citation is the subject of a new sentence, and the fix ties it across the sentence boundary. It also replaces the end-of-sentence space with an ordinary interword space: `end. \ref` measured 33.63pt, `end.~\ref` 32.52pt. (4) PDF hunk in 2506.22564v1: `[comon2008symmetric].` becomes `[comon2008symme`. The text now runs off the page: `indices~\cite{comon2008symmetric}` cannot break, and Overfull warnings go from 187 to 190. This is conditional on the build: the citation is undefined because biber was never run in either build. INFERRED: with resolved citations (`[12]`) this would not occur.
TYPO-016.rationale: MEASURED. I re-ran all 5 cases with LP_FIX_ONLY=TYPO-016 and LP_FIX_TRACE. Edit counts reproduce exactly (281, 398, 250, 297, 358; 1584 in total). Every edit is a same-length ' '->'~' substitution, so I checked each edit's source context by byte position. The hunks_reviewed figure of 1642 counts 58 PDF word hunks plus 1584 source edits. The 58 PDF word hunks are 7+6+4+37+4. I rebuilt 2506.22564v1 because it has 37 hunks and the audit data caps at 25: rc 0/0, and all 37 reproduced. 57 of the 58 PDF hunks are reflow: words reordered around floats and footnotes, superscripts extracted in a different order, hyphenation points moved, and pdftotext spacing artefacts such as `GL(n) × GL(m)` vs `GL(n)×GL(m)` and `d−D.` vs `d − D.`. One hunk is the intended effect exactly: `Theorem` / `17)` split across a float now reads `Theorem 17)`. None of the 58 changes a word, symbol or number, so meaning_changing = 0. Of the 1584 source edits: 1492 follow a word, 50 follow a comma (reference lists such as `Assumptions \ref{a},~\ref{b}`), 15 follow `}`, 3 follow `)`, 5 follow `$`, 1 follows `[`, and 5 follow abbreviations (`e.g.`, `cf.` x3, `Def.`). These are the intended ties. 13 source edits are wrong for context: 5 produce a double space (the space before the edited one is also a space), 1 produces a double space at the start of a line, and 7 tie a new sentence to the end of the previous one. The double-space and sentence-space effects were measured by box widths in a minimal pdflatex document, not in the papers' PDFs, because a word diff cannot see whitespace. The 14th wrong-for-context item is the off-page PDF hunk above. This is a small fraction, but the brief says one wrong-for-context hunk makes a rule UNSAFE, and the defect is systematic, not random. A guard would make the rule allow-listable: skip when the preceding byte is whitespace or `\ `, or starts a line, and skip when the preceding token ends a sentence. INFERRED: `\item \ref` or `& \cite` would also gain a leading tie-space. No sample case contained these.

TYPO-061.what_the_fix_does: Replaces each U+00D7 `×` outside the exempt set (verbatim, comment, url, math) with `$\times$`. It does not look at the surrounding context: moving-argument or PDF-string contexts such as sectioning titles are not excluded. Source: latex-parse/src/validators_l0_typo.ml:2396-2441.
TYPO-061.examples: (1) OUT-OF-SAMPLE, MEASURED on the real corpus paper 2507.08441v1, sections/6_appendix.tex:19. `\subsection{AR Generation with Resolution of 256×256}` becomes `\subsection{AR Generation with Resolution of 256$\times$256}`. The paper loads hyperref. Pristine and fixed both build rc 0, with 0 body word hunks. The fixed build logs 3 `Token not allowed in a PDF string ... removing `\times'` warnings, and the PDF bookmark (outline) entry changes from `AR Generation with Resolution of 256×256` to `AR Generation with Resolution of 256256`, a number that means something different. (2) In sample, fine: 2507.07757v1 `816 × 592 × 816` becomes `816 $\times$ 592 $\times$ 816`; 2507.09183v1 `10×(10w-5s)` in a table becomes `10$\times$(10w-5s)`. (3) In sample, neutral: 2507.10971v1 comparison.tex has 21 instances of `{\color[HTML]{CB0000} ×}`, where × is a table 'no' mark next to `\checkmark`. The math-mode glyph is equivalent in meaning.
TYPO-061.rationale: MEASURED. I re-ran all 5 sampled cases: 7+8+6+14+21 = 56 source edits, which matches edits_alone. I inspected the context of every one. 35 are dimensions or multiplication (`3×3`, `512 × 512`, `10×(...)`), where `$\times$` is correct. 21 are a red × used as a cross mark in a table; the result is visually and semantically equivalent. None of the 56 sampled edits falls in a title or other PDF-string context. All 5 sampled cases had 0 PDF word hunks. That zero says little: pdftotext extracts text × and math × identically, and the word diff never reads PDF bookmarks or metadata. So the audit instrument is blind to this rule's actual failure mode. I grepped the whole corpus (255 papers contain ×) for × inside sectioning commands. That found 2507.08441v1. The fixer does fire there, and I built the paper pristine and fixed: the body text is identical, but the hyperref bookmark changes from `256×256` to `256256`. That is a meaning change in the delivered PDF (its outline), so one meaning-changing hunk makes the rule UNSAFE. The 57 hunks are the 56 sampled edits plus this one; 56 are intended typography and 1 changes meaning. A minimal repro confirms that `×` keeps the bookmark as `256\327256` (the × is preserved), while `$\times$` loses it. The rule could be allow-listed if it skipped `\section`/`\subsection`/`\chapter`/`\caption[...]`/`\title` arguments, or emitted `\texorpdfstring{$\times$}{×}` there. INFERRED: `\title` would affect the PDF metadata in the same way; this was not observed.

VERB-002.what_the_fix_does: Replaces every hard tab inside a verbatim, lstlisting or minted body with a fixed 4 spaces. It ignores the tab's current column (tab stops) and the document's own `tabsize` setting. Source: latex-parse/src/validators_l0.ml:3775-3811.
VERB-002.examples: (1) 2507.04032v1 triangle20250705.tex. The preamble sets `\lstset{... tabsize = 4, columns=fixed ...}`. Inside a MATLAB for-loop, line 3374 `   <TAB>    M2 = eval(M2a0);` and line 3375 `  <TAB>    verify();` render at column 8 in pristine, aligned with the sibling `M1 = eval(M1a0);`. After the fix they have 3+4+4 and 2+4+4 spaces. pdftotext -layout of the rebuilt PDFs shows `            M2 = e v a l ( M2a0 );` becoming `               M2 = e v a l ( M2a0 );` (3 columns further right) and `            verify ();` becoming `              verify ();` (2 columns further right). The same misalignment appears at lines 3150 and 3262 (`verify();`). (2) 2507.10407v1 sample-sigconf.tex. A Macaulay2 lambda body (`<TAB>tvals := ...` ... `<TAB>)`) under listings' default tabsize 8 renders at column 8, nested inside the enclosing `    );` at column 4. After the fix, the body renders at column 4, the same level as the closing `);`. The printed nesting is flattened, and all 6 lines shift in the layout diff.
VERB-002.rationale: MEASURED. I re-ran both cases (20 and 6 edits, matching edits_alone) and rebuilt both; each builds rc 0 pristine and fixed. There are 0 PDF word hunks because the word diff cannot see whitespace, so the audit's 0 is uninformative for this rule. The pdftotext -layout diff shows the effect. In 2507.04032v1, 16 of the 20 edits are tabs at a column that is a multiple of 4, where 4 spaces equals the author's declared tabsize=4, so the render is unchanged: intended. The other 4 are tabs after 2 or 3 leading spaces. They now render 2-3 columns off, visibly misindenting code in a published listing where the author's alignment was correct. In 2507.10407v1, all 6 edits change the rendered indentation from 8 (listings default) to 4, collapsing a nesting level against the closing `);`. I counted these as wrong for context. That is a weaker case than 2507.04032v1, because 4 might be what the author typed in their editor. The fix substitutes a hard-coded width for tab-stop semantics, so it changes how code in a published PDF is laid out, and in the tabsize=4 paper it is plainly wrong. Correct behaviour would expand each tab to the next multiple of the document's effective `tabsize` (or 8), taking the column into account. INFERRED, not observed in the sample: listings of whitespace-significant code (Makefile recipes need literal tabs; Python mixes tabs and spaces) would print code that is wrong if copied.

SPC-009.what_the_fix_does: Deletes a `~` (or a U+00A0 non-breaking space) found at the very start of a source line (validators_l0.ml r_spc_009). It does not look at what comes before it, such as whether the previous line ends in a `%` comment or whether the `~` is holding up a `\\` or acting as a spacer.
SPC-009.examples:
(1) MEASURED BUILD BREAK, 2507.05913v1 (ICML-Workshop-SBoN_v2.tex): the source has a blank line, then `~\`, then a blank line. The fix leaves `\` at the start of a paragraph. Pristine build: rc 0. With LP_FIX_ONLY=SPC-009: rc 1, `! LaTeX Error: There's no line here to end.`, no PDF. 2507.00737v1 has the same `

~\\	extbf{...}` pattern (break INFERRED, not compiled). (2) MEASURED WORD FUSION, 2506.13950v1: the source is `$\mathbf{y}^{(r)} \in \partial \mathcal{D}$.%~These terms...
~The second`. The `~` is the only space between the sentences, so the PDF goes from `∂D. The second` to `∂D.The second`, and likewise `Rk . Having` becomes `Rk .Having`. A synthetic `foo bar.%c
~Next` compiles to `foo bar.Next`. (3) 2506.23344v1 and 2507.03714v1: `\end{subfigure}
~
 egin{subfigure}`. The `~` is a deliberate spacer between subfigures and the fix deletes it. (4) 2507.08658v1: deliberate `~` padding in the first column of a table is removed (24 layout lines change). (5) 2507.09851v1 `\affiliation{%
~\` and 2506.23790v1 ` egin{problem}[..]
~
 egin{description}` are layout idioms that the fix destroys.
SPC-009.rationale: MEASURED. I reviewed all 9 PDF word hunks in the audit (2 are word fusions; the other 7 are an algorithm re-layout, and a page render of 2506.23249 shows the content unchanged). I also traced 12 audit source edits in papers outside the sample (2506.13950 and 2507.08658, 4 each, plus 4 of 2506.13950's in context) and all 105 pass-1 source edits in a 500-paper random sample of the corpus (seed 7). The rule breaks a real paper that compiled before, fuses sentences in another, and deletes deliberate `~` spacers or `~\\` idioms in 6 more papers. The harmless majority are 42 `~` in empty table cells, 36 stray U+00A0 characters in one algorithm, and `\n~\cite` double spaces. Even there, deleting the `~` rather than moving it removes the tie the author asked for.

MATH-082.what_the_fix_does: Inside math, rewrites each `\!\!` as `\!`. Because the fixer repeats until nothing changes, a run of N `\!` shrinks all the way down to a single `\!`. Measured in the trace of 2507.04032v1: a 12-long run `\qquad&\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!` is cut down over passes 1 to 4.
MATH-082.examples: (1) 2507.04032v1: a deliberate `\qquad&` followed by 12 `\!` in align* (outdenting by -2em) becomes a single `\!`, which shifts 3 displays. (2) 2507.09052v1: `\bar{\alpha}_t\!\!=\!\!\prod` is deliberate tightening, and the PDF changes from `ᾱt=` to `ᾱt =`. (3) 2506.19142v1: `\!\times\!\!\!\! \prod_{m:...}` is hand-kerned, and the positions of the product's subscripts change in the PDF. (4) 2507.09627v1: tightened equations get wider and a figure and a subsection move. I rebuilt all 33 hunks, not just the capped 25: the character multiset of the PDF text is identical, so this is pure reflow. (5) Sample: 2507.09848v1 uses the idiom `n_{m~\!\! n}` 1910 times, and 2506.17416v1 has `\int_x^{x+h} \!\!\!\! \Sigma`. The textbook `\int\!\!\int` becomes `\int\!\int` (synthetic, measured).
MATH-082.rationale: MEASURED. I reviewed 37 audit PDF hunks (all of 2507.09627's 33 were rebuilt), 61 audit source edits, and 2208 pass-1 edits in 22 papers of the 500-paper sample. The runs are 2 to 17 `\!` long, and runs of 3 or more are collapsed completely. Not one case looks like a typo. Every one is the author's deliberate negative kerning or alignment trick, which the fix silently undoes. No characters are changed, so this is 0 meaning-changing, but it is wrong for its context in every sampled case. The rule's premise, 'overwhelmingly a typo', is refuted by the corpus.

SPC-028.what_the_fix_does: Collapses every run of 2 or more `~` into a single `~`. It is guarded against verbatim and \url, but it collapses inside math, table cells, \xrightarrow{...}, \underline{...} and author blocks.
SPC-028.examples: (1) 2507.09808v1: in hand-written pseudo-code, `3 ~~$x^*(\mu_k)\leftarrow...$` becomes `3 ~$x^*...$`, so the loop-body indentation that shows the nesting is lost. 2506.17575v1 has the same problem with `~~~ 6.1 Solve`. (2) 2507.06295v1: `\xrightarrow{~~~~~}`, a deliberately long arrow in a chain of maps, becomes a short `\xrightarrow{~}`. (3) 2507.04427v1: in a bibliography URL, `Sokal\underline{~~}20091109.pdf` (a hand-drawn underscore) is halved. (4) 2507.08772v1, 2507.08980v1, 2506.14605v1, 2507.10741v1: deliberate `~~~` separators in author and affiliation blocks. The audit PDF shows the affiliation superscript `4` moving. (5) 2507.09242v1: `~~ + Angular Corrections`, a deliberate sub-row indent in an ablation table, is collapsed. 2507.07978v1: run-in headings `\textbf{X.}~~ Text`. The only clearly intended fixes are `Algorithm~~\ref`, `Definition~~\ref` and `include:~~(a)` (3).
SPC-028.rationale: MEASURED at source level on all 121 edits: 88 pass-1 edits in 26 sample papers plus 33 audit-only edits. I also reviewed the 2 audit PDF hunks. Repeated `~` is how LaTeX authors ask for fixed, unbreakable extra space, and in about 97% of cases the fix removes deliberate indentation, padding, arrow length or separators. It never changes words, but it is wrong for its context almost everywhere.

SPC-021.what_the_fix_does: Deletes one space before `:` outside math (math-range and verbatim/url/lstlisting guarded), repeating until no space is left before the colon. There is no language filter.
SPC-021.examples: (1) 2507.10409v2: the definition symbol `$\kappa$ := effective...` and `$S$ := FLOPs/clock` become `κ:=` and `S:=`, an asymmetric binary relation. This shows in the audit PDF. (2) 2507.04604v1: in table cells of projective points on a modular curve, `(1 : 1 : 0)`, `(3 : -29 : 1)` and so on become `(1: 1: 0)`. Mathematical ratio notation is corrupted 16 times. (3) 2507.10667v1: the ratio `(a 1 : 5--10 mass ratio` becomes `1: 5–10`. (4) 2506.16341v1: inside a custom listing environment `\begin{cprog}`, the displayed C code `? A\n : B` (a ternary operator) is edited. (5) 2507.08329v1: inside a `vquote` environment (verbatimwrite-based, which the guard does not recognise) the verbatim text is edited 7 times. That file is not compiled in this paper, so the risk is INFERRED. 2506.19568v1 also edits `\texttt{ GD: #1 :DG }` markers.
SPC-021.rationale: MEASURED. I reviewed 27 audit PDF hunks (2506.20048 table labels and 2506.24071 `Case 1 :` are intended; the 2507.10409 `:=` hunks are wrong) and 161 source edits: 135 pass-1 edits in 43 sample papers plus 26 audit-only edits. Most edits are ordinary prose colons, which are fine. But the rule cannot tell a punctuation colon from ratio or projective notation, the `:=` definition symbol, or code inside user-defined listing and verbatim environments. 24 edits had no visible effect (inside `\iffalse`, after `\end{document}`, or inside undetected math). INFERRED: with languages=[], French text set without babel-french would lose the space French requires before a colon.

SPC-025.what_the_fix_does: Deletes the space before `\dots` or U+2026, anywhere in the file. It is not math-aware and not context-aware: `, \dots,` becomes `,\dots,`.
SPC-025.examples: (1) 2507.10699v1 (audit PDF): `$d_7$-$a_1$, \dots, $d_4$-$a_2$` goes from `a1 , . . . , d4` to `a1 ,. . . , d4`, which is wrong in an enumerated list. (2) 2507.10005v1 (sample): `$1$, $2$, \dots, $8$` and `$128$, $64$, \dots, $16$` become `,\dots,`. (3) 2506.18512v1: `\{disease1; disease2; \dots\}` in an output-format template becomes `;\dots`. (4) 2507.09953v1: `\verb"\balpha" \dots\ \verb"\bomega"`, a symmetric range, loses its left space. (5) 2507.06724v1: the running head `transformation  \dots` loses both spaces over two passes, and the PDF shows `ζ-TRANSFORMATION . . .` becoming `ζ-TRANSFORMATION. . .` 5 times. I counted this as borderline and scored it intended.
SPC-025.rationale: MEASURED. I reviewed the 7 audit PDF hunks and 27 source edits: 21 pass-1 edits in 7 sample papers plus 6 audit-only edits. In the most common textual use, an elided list `a, \dots, b`, the fix is wrong, because the space after the comma is correct. 12 edits are in math macros, where they have no effect.

SPC-016.what_the_fix_does: Deletes one space before `;` outside math (verbatim/url/control-space guarded), repeating until no space is left before the semicolon. There is no language filter.
SPC-016.examples: (1) WRONG, 2506.18011v1: in a `quote` environment, a verbatim test-set instance shown as tokenizer output, `"[CLS] ... sad is about all i can say ; this movie ... [SEP]"`, becomes `say; this`. The paper then analyses nearest tokens position by position, so the spaced token is data and must not be edited (source measured; the PDF effect is deterministic). (2) Intended: 2507.02089v1 (audit PDF) `\rangle$ ; $\hat V` becomes `⟩;`, and 2507.05548v1 `for Case 1 ;` becomes `Case 1;`. (3) Borderline: 2507.05550v2, a bibliography series statement `Progress in mathematics ; v. 45`, is catalogue (ISBD) punctuation copied verbatim. (4) No visible effect: TikZ path terminators in 2507.10170v1 and 2507.02347v1, and one edit inside an undetected math environment `aligni*` in 2507.11274v1.
SPC-016.rationale: MEASURED, but on a small sample. I reviewed all 2 audit PDF hunks and 15 source edits (12 pass-1 edits in 10 of the 500 sample papers plus 3 audit edits). Fourteen are fine. One is wrong for its context: it edits quoted model input and data. Under the 'one wrong hunk' rule the verdict is unsafe. Even without that case, 15 edits would be too few to certify the rule safe. INFERRED: no language filter (babel-french re-inserts the French space automatically, so the risk is limited to French text set without it).

SPC-032.what_the_fix_does: On a line whose leading whitespace mixes U+00A0 and ASCII spaces, replaces the whole leading run with ASCII spaces. A line made only of NBSPs and spaces therefore becomes a whitespace-only line, which TeX reads as a blank line, i.e. a paragraph break.
SPC-032.examples:
(1) The only corpus case, 2506.23249v1 (35 edits, in both the audit and the 500-paper sample): U+00A0 indentation inside algorithmic. I rendered page 22 pristine and fixed: the same 39 algorithm lines and the same content. The fix removes the stray empty-line gaps that the NBSPs caused, and line 33 now fits on one line. All 24 audit PDF hunks are pdftotext re-ordering of line numbers. (2) MEASURED ON SYNTHETIC INPUT: `First sentence of para
\xa0 
second sentence.` compiles to one paragraph pristine but to TWO paragraphs after SPC-032, because the NBSP line becomes blank. The real paper has the same shape three times (`\xa0 \xa0 \xa0 \xa0\xa0
` at offsets 85741, 86248 and 86501), where it happened to fall between `\State` lines and was harmless.
SPC-032.rationale: The corpus evidence is thin but clean: 1 paper out of more than 500 sampled, 35 edits and 24 PDF hunks, all intended or improving, verified by render. The edit does have a demonstrated failure mode, however. Turning a non-blank NBSP line into a blank line inserts a \par, which splits a paragraph in running text; this was measured on a synthetic reproduction of a line shape the real paper contains. With n=1 paper, the corpus cannot show the rule is safe, and the known mechanism changes document structure. Under 'when in doubt: UNSAFE' the verdict is unsafe. If the fix skipped lines with nothing after the whitespace, it could be re-measured.

RO-001.what_the_fix_does: Replaces every cedilla letter (Ş ş Ţ ţ, U+015E/015F/0162/0163) with its comma-below form (Ș ș Ț ț), anywhere in the source. In the sample there was no check on context or language: the rule is tagged languages=["ro"] but it fired on a Turkish thesis that declares no language (validators_l0.ml:5438-5482).
RO-001.examples: 2507.09217v1 (MSc.tex, Turkish abstract 'ÖZETÇE'; 23 source edits in the trace): 'işlev' -> 'ișlev', 'artırılmış' -> 'artırılmıș', 'çeşitli' -> 'çeșitli', 'karşı' -> 'karșı', 'şekilde' -> 'șekilde'. Turkish is written with the CEDILLA ş, so all 20 PDF hunks swap correct Turkish spelling for Romanian letters. I rendered page 5 of the fixed PDF and it visibly shows comma-below ș all through the abstract. pdftotext shows these as 's,'; the ', karsı' token in the diff is an extraction artefact, not an extra comma. || 2507.00681v1: 'Mustaţă' -> 'Mustață' (a Romanian surname, correct and intended). I rendered the fixed PDF: the glyph is a proper t with comma-below. pdftotext shows 'Mustat, ă', which is only how the text is extracted.
RO-001.rationale: MEASURED: in 1 of the 2 sampled papers, all 20 hunks of that paper are wrong for their context. The fix changes the correct Turkish ş to the Romanian ș throughout a Turkish abstract, which I confirmed visually in the rendered PDF (compiled rc=0, 0 missing-character warnings). The other paper (a Romanian name) is a correct refinement. INFERRED: the same corruption would hit any Turkish, Azerbaijani, Kurdish, Tatar or Gagauz text, and any name spelt with a cedilla, whenever the paper declares no language. The rule applies to every ş/ţ with no context at all.

ENC-018.what_the_fix_does: Replaces the non-breaking hyphen U+2011 with an ordinary ASCII '-'. It skips math, \url, and (measured on a synthetic probe) verbatim, \verb, \href, \label and \input arguments. The words and glyphs stay the same; only the line-breaking changes, because the hyphen can now end a line.
ENC-018.examples: 2507.08801v1: 'AR‑DF requires' -> 'AR-|DF' now splits across two lines. I rendered page 9 and the acronym 'AR-DF' is broken at the line end, which is exactly what the author's U+2011 prevented (wrong for context). || 2506.21680v1: 'low-light' -> 'lowlight' and 'glove-based' -> 'glovebased'. pdftotext -raw shows these are 'low-' / 'glove-' at a line end, joined back up by pdftotext, so the PDF words are unchanged (layout only; I counted these as intended typography). || 2507.11025v1: 'pseudo-target' -> 'pseudotarget' (the same line-end dehyphenation artefact). || 2506.17696v1 and 2507.03184v1: 0 word hunks.
ENC-018.rationale: MEASURED: none of the 4 hunks changes meaning, and 5/5 papers compile identically (rc 0 -> 0, same page counts). U+2011 already renders as a hyphen in the pristine builds, with 0 'Missing character' or 'Unicode character' warnings, so under the pinned pdflatex the fix buys nothing typographically. What it does do is remove the author's no-break constraint. In 1 of 4 hunks that splits an acronym ('AR-/DF') across a line, which a careful author would not want. The allow-list criterion is 'right in EVERY sampled case', so this rule fails it. It is not a meaning corruption: it is a zero-benefit edit with one measured wrong-for-context outcome. If the owner accepts line-break-only regressions, it would be the least harmful of the four.

STYLE-023.what_the_fix_does: Escapes any '%' that comes straight after a digit ('50%' -> '50\%'), outside verbatim, \verb, url and math. The digit guard cannot tell a literal percent from a comment marker that follows a digit. That includes a macro parameter such as '#1%' or '#2%', the standard end-of-line space-suppressing '%' in a definition, and a comment written after a number.
STYLE-023.examples: 2507.06225v1 (article.tex:39): '20B25% Finite automorphism groups of algebraic, geometric, or combinatorial structures' -> '20B25\% Finite...'. A source COMMENT becomes visible text in the MSC classification: 'Secondary: ... 20B25% Finite automorphism groups ... structures .' (meaning-changing, adds words). || 2506.14026v1 (hyperelliptic_model.tex:34, biblatex \newbibmacro): '#1%' -> '#1\%'. A stray '%' is printed after bibliography titles: 'database”.' -> 'database”%.' (wrong for context, adds a symbol). || 2506.22564v1 (main.tex:109, \DeclarePairedDelimiterX{\infdivx}): '#2%' -> '#2\%'. 0 PDF hunks only because the macro is never used; any use would print '%' inside the math (a latent defect, not counted). || 2507.09949v1: '95% SOC classification accuracy.' -> '95\%'. This restores text the author's unescaped '%' had silently commented out (intended; the only correct case). || Synthetic probe: '\newcommand\foo[1]{#1%' -> '#1\%' (reproduced).
STYLE-023.rationale: MEASURED: 5 source edits across the 5 sampled papers. 1 is a correct fix, 1 exposes a comment as body text, 1 prints a stray '%' in a bibliography, 1 corrupts a macro definition that is unused in that paper, and 1 is the synthetic reproduction. A digit before '%' is the ordinary case for '#1%' and '#2%' in macro definitions and for comments after MSC codes or numbers, so the guard fails on a common idiom, not an edge case. The rule's own comment claims the digit guard is 'cascade-proof'. That is true only with respect to TYPO-014; it is refuted for macro parameters and comments.

CHAR-016.what_the_fix_does: Replaces full-width CJK punctuation (、 。 ： ； ！ ？) with ASCII (, . : ; ! ?) when it is outside math and is_ascii_context holds. The full-width comma and full stop are handed to CJK-001/002.
CHAR-016.examples: 2506.20426v1 (ModulatedCat.tex:111): '\CJKfamily{gbsn}(徐斐、张懋胤)' -> '(徐斐,张懋胤)'. The ideographic enumeration comma between two Chinese names, inside a CJK font run, is replaced by a cramped ASCII comma. I rendered both PDFs and the fixed one visibly shows '徐斐,张懋胤' with a Latin comma squeezed between the ideographs.
CHAR-016.rationale: MEASURED: 1 of 1 sampled hunks is wrong for its context. The character sits between two CJK ideographs inside \CJKfamily, which is exactly the 'genuinely-CJK run' the rule's comment says is exempt, yet is_ascii_context let it through. The sample is only one paper (the rule reached a single preserved paper), but a single wrong-for-context hunk is enough to fail the criterion. INFERRED: the same thing happens wherever CJK text follows a Latin-script context such as a parenthesis or a command, because the context test evidently looks at ASCII neighbours such as '(' or the \CJKfamily argument.

SPC-008.what_the_fix_does: Deletes leading spaces/tabs on the first line of a paragraph (a line after a blank line), except \item lines. Offsets inside the exempt set (built-in verbatim_envs list, comment, url, math) are dropped.
SPC-008.examples: MEASURED on a constructed document (allowC/c1.py). Inside a \lstnewenvironment{python} listing, after a blank line: `    z = 2.   # three` -> `z = 2.   # three`. Inside a \DefineVerbatimEnvironment{code}{Verbatim} block: `    return x.` -> `return x.`. The printed Python code is dedented, which changes the program's block structure. The pixel diff and the pdftotext -layout diff both show it. The 5 real sampled papers had 0 word hunks and 0 layout lines changed.
SPC-008.rationale:
MEASURED: in ordinary text the rule changes nothing, because TeX already skips leading spaces in state N. The exempt layer, however, only knows the fixed verbatim_envs list (validators_common.ml:677). Environments the author defines as verbatim (\lstnewenvironment, \DefineVerbatimEnvironment, 
ewtcblisting, 
ewminted, beamer semiverbatim, pythontex pycode) are not exempt, so the fix removes code indentation that is typeset (or, for pycode, executed). \lstnewenvironment, \DefineVerbatimEnvironment and 
ewtcblisting together appear in about 9 of the 2961 corpus papers (grep). A defined_verbatim_env_names helper already exists (validators_common.ml:1362) but compute_verbatim_comment_url_ranges does not call it.

TYPO-018.what_the_fix_does: Collapses every run of 2 or more spaces to one space outside the exempt set. Also applies at line start, so it removes indentation.
TYPO-018.examples: MEASURED (allowC/c1.py), inside \lstnewenvironment and \DefineVerbatimEnvironment listings: `    y = 1.  # comment` -> ` y = 1. # comment`; `\treturn x    +  y` -> `\treturn x + y`; `    z = 2.   # three` -> ` z = 2. # three`. The rendered code's indentation and alignment collapse (pixel and layout diff). The 5 real sampled papers had 0 hunks. Those papers carried 290 to 2852 edits each, all in ordinary text where TeX already collapses spaces.
TYPO-018.rationale: MEASURED: this is the same hole in the custom-verbatim exempt layer as SPC-008. Outside it, collapsing spaces is a no-op for TeX. INFERRED further hazards: a Python pythontex pycode or sagetex block, where the collapsed indentation is executed; and \obeyspaces contexts.

TYPO-055.what_the_fix_does: Replaces each text-mode `\,\,` with `\,`. Math is exempt. The converging --apply-fixes repeats the replacement until a whole run of thin spaces becomes a single `\,`.
TYPO-055.examples: MEASURED on real paper 2506.14940v1 (Mult_0_most_2_arxiv_2025_06_17.tex, 79 edits). The author indents table sub-rows by hand with thin-space runs: line 1132 `\,\,\,\,\, \,\,\,\,\, $p=2$& $\om_2$&` becomes `\, \, $p=2$& $\om_2$&` after the fixer. Every such hand-built indent in that table is destroyed. The audit recorded 0 word hunks and 0 layout lines because pdftotext does not see thin spaces. MEASURED synthetic (allowC/c2.py): `x\\,\,y` (a line break, a comma, then a thin space) matches, so a thin space is removed, although the producer comment claims this cannot match. `1\,\,000` -> `1\,000`; the pixels differ.
TYPO-055.rationale: The premise that a double thin space is always a typo is false. Authors use runs of \, deliberately to space and align by hand, and the fixpoint loop collapses a run of any length. The measured real-paper case is a visible layout change against the author's intent, and the audit's pdftotext metric cannot detect it.

SCRIPT-021.what_the_fix_does: Inside math, rewrites a fully braced `_{B}^{C}` as `^{C}_{B}`, repeating until a fixpoint.
SCRIPT-021.examples: MEASURED (allowC/c3.py) with \usepackage{tensor}: `\tensor{R}{_{a}^{b}_{c}^{d}}` -> `\tensor{R}{^{b}^{d}_{a}_{c}}`, and pdftotext shows `Rabcd` -> `Rbdac`. The staggered index order R_a^b_c^d becomes R^{bd}_{ac}, a different tensor. `T\indices{_{\mu}^{\nu}}` -> `T\indices{^{\nu}_{\mu}}` (T_mu^nu becomes T^nu_mu). Both compile with rc 0, and the pixels differ. Also MEASURED: it rewrites `$x_{a}^{b}$` inside a \lstnewenvironment listing. The 5 real sampled papers had 0 hunks.
SCRIPT-021.rationale: The claim that the result renders identically holds only for plain TeX scripts. In the tensor package's \tensor and \indices, the source order of _ and ^ IS the typeset index order, which carries meaning in general-relativity and physics papers. 13 of the 2961 corpus papers load tensor. INFERRED as well: match_brace treats any brace preceded by a backslash as escaped, so `\\}` (a line break followed by a closing brace) is mis-scanned.

SPC-011.what_the_fix_does: Strips spaces and tabs before a newline in regions that a raw `$$` toggle scanner considers display math. It uses no exempt filtering at all: a `$$` inside a comment, verbatim or a listing flips the toggle.
SPC-011.examples: MEASURED (allowC/c8.py): in a STANDARD `\begin{lstlisting}[showtabs=true]` whose code contains `$$`, the trailing tabs in `a\t` and `b\t` are stripped, and the rendered tab markers disappear (pixels differ). The same happens in a custom \lstnewenvironment with showtabs (c7.py). Also MEASURED (c2.py): trailing spaces and tabs in a plain verbatim block or a $$ display leave the pixels unchanged, because TeX's line reader strips them there. The 5 real sampled papers had 0 hunks.
SPC-011.rationale: The fix is almost always a no-op, because TeX strips trailing spaces at input. It is not provably a no-op: the producer is not gated by any exempt range, and tabs survive into listings where the author has asked for them to be shown. The failure is cosmetic and niche (it needs showtabs), but it is a measured visible change inside a code listing. Cheap repair: restrict the edit to spaces only and route it through mk_result_with_fix_exempt; stripping trailing spaces only is provably a no-op at TeX's line reader.

STRUCT-003.what_the_fix_does: Replaces each tab character with one space outside the exempt set.
STRUCT-003.examples: MEASURED (allowC/c1.py): in \lstnewenvironment{python}, `\treturn x    +  y` -> ` return x    +  y`, so the listing's tab indentation of 8 columns becomes 1 column (layout and pixels differ, and Python block structure changes). The same happens to `\ttabbed    here` in a \DefineVerbatimEnvironment{code}{Verbatim} block. The 5 real sampled papers had 0 hunks (817 to 1866 edits in prose, where a tab and a space are both catcode 10).
STRUCT-003.rationale: MEASURED: this is the custom-verbatim exempt hole again. INFERRED further hazard: filecontents is not exempt, so tab-separated data written for pgfplots or csvsimple with `col sep=tab`, or a Makefile, would be corrupted.

SCRIPT-018.what_the_fix_does: Inside math, rewrites `^\circ` (when not followed by a letter) as `^{\circ}`. Only verbatim, comment and url regions are exempt.
SCRIPT-018.examples: MEASURED (allowC/c4.py): inside a \lstnewenvironment{tex} listing that shows LaTeX source, `$x^\circ$` -> `$x^{\circ}$`, so the printed code changes (pixels and pdftotext differ). In real math the result renders identically; the 5 real sampled papers had 0 hunks.
SCRIPT-018.rationale: The rule has no intrinsic hazard that I could find: a braced single-macro superscript renders identically, and the not-followed-by-a-letter check protects \circledcirc. The only hazard is the shared one: find_math_ranges treats `$..$` inside a user-defined verbatim environment as math, and the vcu exempt list does not know that environment. The rule becomes safe once the exempt layer honours defined_verbatim_env_names. The trigger is rare (a LaTeX-source listing in a custom environment), but the owner's rule is one wrong hunk makes a rule unsafe.

TYPO-017.what_the_fix_does: Rewrites `\<accent>{<letter>}` as `\<accent><letter>` for the accents ' ^ ` " ~ = . outside the exempt set.
TYPO-017.examples: MEASURED (allowC/c3.py): inside a \lstnewenvironment{tex} listing, `Caf\'{e}` -> `Caf\'e`; pdftotext shows `\ ’{ e }` -> `\ ’ e`, so the displayed source code changes. In prose, `Caf\'{e}` -> `Caf\'e` renders identically. The 5 real sampled papers had 0 hunks.
TYPO-017.rationale: Removing the braces is equivalent in prose (checked by reasoning for tabbing, \uppercase and makeindex; control symbols are also protected by Fix_guard region 1, except that this rule is on its control_symbol_aware list). The only hazard found is the shared custom-verbatim exempt hole. That makes it unsafe as implemented, and repairable centrally.

SPC-002.what_the_fix_does: Empties any line that contains only spaces, tabs or CR. Built-in verbatim, comment, url and math regions are exempt.
SPC-002.examples: MEASURED (allowC/c6.py, c7.py): in prose, \obeyspaces\obeylines, a fancyvrb Verbatim with showspaces, and a listing without showtabs, the pixels are unchanged (TeX's line reader already strips trailing spaces). In a custom \lstnewenvironment with `showtabs=true`, a tab-only line `\t\t` -> `` removes the visible tab markers (pixels differ). The 5 real sampled papers had 0 hunks (151 to 855 edits).
SPC-002.rationale: This is the lowest-severity entry: it is essentially pure source hygiene. The only visible change I could produce needs a custom listings environment with showtabs=true and a tab-only line. It changes no words, but it is a context where the fix is wrong. Cheap repair: only empty lines that contain SPACES (and CR) only. Those are provably no-ops, because TeX strips trailing spaces before tokenising, so the input line is identical. With that restriction the rule would be safe.

SPC-031.what_the_fix_does: Collapses a period followed by 3 or more spaces to a period and one space, outside the exempt set.
SPC-031.examples: MEASURED (allowC/c1.py): inside \lstnewenvironment{python}, `    z = 2.   # three` -> `    z = 2. # three`, and inside a \DefineVerbatimEnvironment{code}{Verbatim} block, `    return x.   # aligned` -> `    return x. # aligned`. Comment alignment in the rendered code is lost (layout and pixels differ). The 5 real sampled papers had 0 hunks.
SPC-031.rationale: The fix is a no-op in prose, because TeX collapses spaces. It is visible in user-defined verbatim environments, which the exempt layer does not recognise: the shared hole again.

STYLE-015.what_the_fix_does: Deletes the extra spaces after a period followed by 2 or more spaces, outside the exempt set.
STYLE-015.examples: MEASURED (allowC/c1.py): inside a custom listing, `    y = 1.  # comment` -> `    y = 1. # comment`, `    z = 2.   # three` -> `    z = 2. # three`, and `return x.   # aligned` -> `return x. # aligned` (pixels and layout differ). The 5 real sampled papers had 0 hunks.
STYLE-015.rationale: Same as SPC-031: a no-op in prose, but it corrupts code alignment in user-defined verbatim environments that the exempt list does not cover.

PL-001.what_the_fix_does: Replaces the ASCII space before ` r.`, ` nr ` or ` s.` with a UTF-8 non-breaking space (bytes C2 A0), outside the exempt set. Fix_guard drops non-ASCII replacements in documents that declare a legacy inputenc (reading of fix_guard.ml).
PL-001.examples: MEASURED on real papers: under LP_FIX_ONLY the rule fired on 5 ENGLISH papers. The edits are `$t=$ 2 s.` -> `2<NBSP>s.` (2506.17726v1) and `$L$ s.t.` -> `$L$<NBSP>s.t.` (2507.10976v1 and others). These are harmless and even reasonable. MEASURED synthetic (allowC/c4.py): the text ` in r. 5` inside a \lstnewenvironment listing gets an NBSP, and the compile goes from rc 0 to rc 1 with `Invalid UTF-8 byte sequence` (listings splits the multi-byte character). INFERRED: Python code such as `x = s.split()` inside a custom listing triggers this directly.
PL-001.rationale: The rule is supposed to be Polish-only (languages = ["pl"]), yet it applied to English papers in the fixer run. So the language gate is either bypassed under LP_FIX_ONLY or not applied on the --apply-fixes path. That is worth checking separately. More seriously, it inserts a non-ASCII byte into user-defined listings, which the exempt layer does not recognise, and that is a measured compile break.

MATH-053.what_the_fix_does: Inside math, deletes the space in `\left( `. Only verbatim, comment and url regions are exempt.
MATH-053.examples: MEASURED (allowC/c3.py): inside a \lstnewenvironment{tex} listing, `$\left( x \right)$` -> `$\left(x \right)$`, so the printed source changes (pixels differ). In real math the space is ignored; the 5 real sampled papers (57 to 292 edits) had 0 hunks.
MATH-053.rationale: The rule has no intrinsic hazard: math-mode spaces are ignored and `(` is not a letter, so no token merges. Its only hazard is the shared custom-verbatim hole, because find_math_ranges sees `$..$` inside a user-defined listing as math. It is repairable centrally.

MATH-015.what_the_fix_does: Inside math, renames `\stackrel{` to `\overset{`. It does not check that amsmath is loaded.
MATH-015.examples: MEASURED synthetic (allowC/c2.py). (1) An article without amsmath: `$a \stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=} b$` -> `\overset`, and the compile goes from rc 0 to rc 1 (undefined control sequence). (2) With amsmath: `$x\stackrel{\circ}{A}y$`, `$\stackrel{\circ}{A}\cap B$` -> \overset, and the spacing changes (pdftotext `x A y` -> `xAy`, `A ∩B` -> `A ∩ B`), because \stackrel is always a relation while \overset takes the class of its base. (3) It rewrites \stackrel inside a custom listing. The real sample (e.g. 2506.20910v1 `\stackrel{(i)}{=}`, 2507.10160v1 `\stackrel{i.i.d.}{\sim}`) used relation bases only, with 0 hunks. Of the 295 corpus papers that use \stackrel, 3 show no amsmath or mathtools by grep; the one of those that got an edit (2506.17688v1) still compiled, so its amsmath presumably comes from somewhere my grep missed.
MATH-015.rationale: The package dependency is intrinsic: \overset needs amsmath, and I measured the compile break. The spacing also changes whenever the base is not a relation, as with the very common interior notation \stackrel{\circ}{A}. On top of that comes the shared custom-verbatim hole.

SPC-020.what_the_fix_does: Deletes every TAB byte that its own naive $-toggle scanner thinks is inside math (vcu-exempt only; it does NOT use find_math_ranges, does not honour \$, and a single $ anywhere flips state for the rest of the file).
SPC-020.examples: MEASURED on synthetic docs (pristine vs LP_FIX_ONLY=SPC-020, pdflatex + pdftotext): (1) 'It costs \$5 and<TAB>then some ... more<TAB>words' -> 'andthen', 'morewords'. The \$ toggles the scanner into 'math', prose tabs are deleted and the PDF words merge (rc 0 both sides, silent). (2) '$a \leq<TAB>b$' -> '$a \leqb$', so pdflatex goes rc 0 -> 1 with 'Undefined control sequence' and no PDF. The tab ended the control word. All 5 real sampled cases (2506.24071, 2507.00681, 2507.00934, 2507.04032, 2507.09737) happened to give 0 word hunks.
SPC-020.rationale: MEASURED hazards: the sample was clean only because it contained no \$ and no control-word<TAB>letter. Tab-as-token-separator after a control word is ordinary author input, and so is \$ in prose. The docstring's 'safe-by-construction' claim is false on both counts.

MATH-061.what_the_fix_does: In math, rewrites \log_<digits><alnum> to \log_{<all digits>}..., which changes the subscript's scope whenever the digit run is longer than one digit.
MATH-061.examples: Real sample 2507.04581: 4 edits '\log_2k' -> '\log_{2}k' render identically (intended, harmless). MEASURED synthetic: '$\log_210 \approx 3.32$' (log base 2 of 10) -> '$\log_{210}$' (log base 210), and '$\log_23$ is irrational' -> '$\log_{23}$'. pdftotext shows 'log2 10' -> 'log210' and 'log2 3' -> 'log23'. The mathematics changes and it still compiles.
MATH-061.rationale: MEASURED meaning change. The only edits that change rendering are the multi-digit ones, and for those the PDF the author proofread shows log_2(10), which is a plausible intent. The fix silently rewrites the base. The zero-diff sample only had single-digit bases, which are no-ops. Also, pdftotext word diffs are nearly blind to subscript scope, so zero word hunks is weak evidence for math rules.

TYPO-042.what_the_fix_does: Collapses every run of >= 2 '?' outside math/verbatim/comment/url to a single '?'. This deletes typeset characters.
TYPO-042.examples: Real sample 2506.21741: the journal-template placeholder '{??-????}' (an ISSN/DOI slot) -> '{?-?}'. That is wrong for context; it did not reach the PDF in that build. MEASURED synthetic: '\texttt{a ?? b}' (the C# null-coalescing operator) -> 'a ? b', the ternary, a different operator. 'ISSN ??-????.' -> 'ISSN ?-?.'. 'Really??' -> 'Really?'. All three show in the pdftotext diff.
TYPO-042.rationale: MEASURED: the fix changes printed text, including code in \texttt (only verbatim is exempt) and placeholders. Collapsing an author's '??' is an editorial opinion, not a typographic refinement.

TYPO-027.what_the_fix_does: Collapses every run of >= 2 '!' outside math/verbatim/comment/url to a single '!'. This deletes typeset characters.
TYPO-027.examples: Real sample 2507.11226: '(WE SHOUL DO THIS!!!)' -> '!'. This is an author note that evidently was not typeset (0 hunks). MEASURED synthetic: '\texttt{!!x} coerces to boolean' -> '\texttt{!x}' (double negation becomes negation, so the code's meaning flips), and 'Hurray!!!' -> 'Hurray!'. Both are visible in the pdftotext diff.
TYPO-027.rationale: MEASURED: it rewrites printed text, including code in \texttt, and \texttt is not exempt. The math exemption protects n!! only inside $...$.

CHEM-004.what_the_fix_does: In math, rewrites every '^-'/'^+' whose preceding byte is ASCII letter to '^{-}'/'^{+}' (not just chemical charges: real samples are E^+_{G(R)}, x^-y etc.).
CHEM-004.examples: Real samples (5 papers, 293 pass-1 edits inspected by trace): all were ordinary math superscripts such as 'E^+_{G(R)}' -> 'E^{+}_{G(R)}'. These render identically. They are general math, not charges, contrary to the docstring. MEASURED synthetic hazard: in xy-pic, '\xymatrix{ A \rto^-{f} & B }' (the '-' is xy's label-position marker) -> '\rto^{-}{f}'. The arrow label becomes a minus sign and 'f' is typeset loose next to A ('A / f' becomes 'Af / −' in pdftotext). It compiles, rc 0 on both sides.
CHEM-004.rationale: The ordinary math case is render-identical by TeX grammar (a one-token superscript), so 0 hunks in the sample is expected. But any macro that parses '^' as its own syntax is corrupted silently when the byte before '^' is a letter: xy-pic's \rto/\dto shortcuts, and other diagram packages. Niche, but MEASURED and silent.

REF-011.what_the_fix_does: Inserts \usepackage{hyperref} right after \documentclass when \autoref is used and the MAIN FILE's text shows no hyperref/cleveref. It cannot see hyperref loaded by the class or by a local .sty.
REF-011.examples: Real sample 2507.09242: acmart already loads hyperref, so the insertion was a redundant no-op and wrong for context. MEASURED synthetic: a local ref11sty.sty with '\RequirePackage[colorlinks=true,linkcolor=red]{hyperref}' -> after the fix pdflatex rc 0 -> 1 with 'LaTeX Error: Option clash for package hyperref', no PDF. (The insertion is withheld by Fix_guard only when the line after \documentclass is itself a \usepackage, which is a coincidence and not a guard for this case.)
REF-011.rationale: MEASURED compile break. The rule only fires on compiling papers when \autoref is already defined some other way (class or local sty). That is exactly the case where inserting hyperref early is redundant at best, and an option clash or load-order change at worst.

PKG-011.what_the_fix_does: Inserts \usepackage{booktabs} right after \documentclass when \toprule/\midrule/\bottomrule appears and the main file has no booktabs \usepackage.
PKG-011.examples: Real samples: 2507.09242 (acmart, which loads booktabs), 2507.04481 (booktabs probably loaded via \input{common_defs}), 2507.08329 (doc/elsdoc-cas.tex). All 3 were redundant insertions (0 hunks). MEASURED synthetic: a paper with '\newcommand{\toprule}{\hline\hline}' (and \midrule, \bottomrule) -> after the fix pdflatex rc 0 -> 1 with 'LaTeX Error: Command \toprule already defined', no PDF.
PKG-011.rationale: MEASURED compile break. On a compiling paper \toprule is by definition already defined somewhere (class, local sty, \input, or the author's own \newcommand). Loading booktabs early is either redundant or collides with the author's definition.

CHAR-018.what_the_fix_does: Replaces precomposed ligature codepoints U+FB00-FB04 with their ASCII letters, outside verbatim/comment/url/math. It is NOT limited to typeset text: package arguments are rewritten too.
CHAR-018.examples: Real samples 2506.21739 and 2507.04653: 'Diﬀerence' -> 'Difference' in bibliographies. The same word is extracted, so these are intended. MEASURED synthetic: '\newunicodechar{ﬁ}{fi}' -> '\newunicodechar{fi}{fi}' makes pdflatex go rc 0 -> 1 with 'Package newunicodechar Error: Invalid argument', no PDF. Note that \label{ﬁg}/\ref{ﬁg} are correctly withheld by Fix_guard.
CHAR-018.rationale: MEASURED compile break. A paper containing ligature codepoints under pdflatex often compiles precisely because it declares them (\newunicodechar), and the fix destroys that declaration. The prose rewrite is benign. A guard for \newunicodechar and \DeclareUnicodeCharacter-style arguments would make it a candidate again.

SPC-010.what_the_fix_does: Collapses exactly two spaces between '.' and a capital letter to one, outside the hard-coded verbatim env list, comments, url and math.
SPC-010.examples: Real samples (5 papers, 111-564 edits each): 0 word or layout hunks. In prose TeX already collapses the spaces, so this is pure source hygiene. MEASURED synthetic: '\DefineVerbatimEnvironment{code}{Verbatim}{}' body 'x = a.  B' -> 'x = a. B', and '\lstnewenvironment{py}' body 'y = c.  D' -> 'y = c. D'. The printed code listing changes (pdftotext 'a.   B' -> 'a. B'). Only literal names such as verbatim and lstlisting are exempt; user-defined verbatim environments are not.
SPC-010.rationale: Outside verbatim it is pure hygiene and cannot reach the PDF. It is MEASURED to rewrite author-defined verbatim/listing bodies, which silently changes printed code. It would be safe if gated with defined_verbatim_env_names (which already exists in validators_common.ml).

TYPO-046.what_the_fix_does: Rewrites \begin{math} / \end{math} to $ (and deletes an adjacent empty pair), vcu-exempt.
TYPO-046.examples:
Real sample 2507.10971: a multi-line  egin{math}(Sa \xrightarrow{} ...)\end{math} -> $...$, 0 hunks. MEASURED synthetic stress test, with 0 text diff and rc 0 on both sides: 
ewenvironment{mm}{ egin{math}}{\end{math}} -> {$}{$}; 
ewcommand{\mth}[1]{ egin{math}#1\end{math}}; an array 
ewcolumntype >{ egin{math}}c<{\end{math}}; adjacent '\end{math} egin{math}' -> '$x+y$$z$' (correctly still two inline maths); an empty pair deleted; and 	ext{... egin{math} eta\end{math}...} inside math.
TYPO-046.rationale: No hazard found after trying the adversarial forms I could think of: macro and environment definitions, column types, adjacency ($$ risk), empty pair, and nested \text. INFERRED residuals: a document where $ has a non-math catcode outside the listed verbatim envs, and hyperref PDF-string (bookmark) text. Neither affects the page text.

refutation.evidence:
MEASURED (pristine vs LP_FIX_ONLY=TYPO-046 --apply-fixes, compiled with run_to_fixpoint, pdftotext word diff; harness and cases in /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-dylanpossamai-Library-CloudStorage-Dropbox-Work-Articles-Scripts/6724887f-375f-4639-96cf-722343631c21/scratchpad/typo046/ in syn/, syn.jsonl, corpus.jsonl and m_*/).

Why it happens: the producer only exempts the fixed verbatim_envs list (verbatim, Verbatim, BVerbatim, LVerbatim, lstlisting, minted, alltt, comment, listing, tcblisting) plus \verb, \lstinline, comments and URLs (validators_common.ml:677 and compute_verbatim_comment_url_ranges). It also matches the exact spellings `\begin{math}` and `\end{math}` separately, with no check that they pair up.

A) Printed code in a verbatim environment the author defined is rewritten. The page text changes, and it is wrong in exactly the context where the difference is the point: a paper that shows LaTeX source.
 - syn/lstnew: `\lstnewenvironment{latexcode}{...}{}` containing `The area is \begin{math}\pi r^2\end{math}.` gives rc 0,0. The PDF text changes from `\ begin { math }\ pi r ^2\ end { math }` to `$\ pi r ^2$`. The trace shows 2 edits at offsets 244 and 263.
 - syn/fvrbenv: `\DefineVerbatimEnvironment{code}{Verbatim}{}` gives rc 0,0. The text changes from `The area is \begin{math}\pi r^2\end{math}.` to `The area is $\pi r^2$.`
 - syn/Verbinline: fancyvrb inline `\Verb|\begin{math}x\end{math}|` gives rc 0,0. The text changes from `Write \begin{math}x\end{math} for inline math` to `Write $x$ for inline math`. Only lowercase \verb is exempt.
 - syn/filecont: a `filecontents*` body shown with \VerbatimInput gives rc 0,0. The text changes from `\begin{math}a^2\end{math}` to `$a^2$`.
These patterns do appear in the corpus: lstnewenvironment in 4 papers, newtcblisting in 4, DefineVerbatimEnvironment in 1, \Verb in 1. None of those papers contain \begin{math}, though.

B) Compilation breaks (pristine rc 0, fixed rc 1, no PDF):
 - syn/spacebegin: `\begin {math}x+y\end{math}`. The spaced begin is valid LaTeX but is not matched, so only the end is rewritten, giving `\begin {math}x+y$`. Result: "! LaTeX Error: \begin{math} on input line 3 ended by \end{document}."
 - syn/cmtempty: `\begin{math}%<newline>\end{math}`. The empty-pair guard only recognises adjacent delimiters, so this becomes `$%<newline>$`, which TeX reads as `$$` (display math). Result: "! Missing $ inserted", fatal.

Real corpus: every file containing the trigger was checked. There are 13 such files. The 9 that compile were built both ways (2506.21642v2 with 198 edits, 2507.02165v1 with 180 edits but rc 1 even unfixed, 2507.08520v1 with 20, 2506.12663v1 with 4, and 2507.02759v2, 2507.08909v1, 2506.10830v1, 2507.10971v1, 2507.07949v1 with 2 each). All gave 0 word hunks, 0 layout lines changed and the same page counts. The remaining files have only commented-out occurrences (2507.09560v1 applied 0 edits). So on real papers the rule looks safe. The damage above is measured on minimal documents that use realistic constructs, not found in a corpus paper.

Safe on test (MEASURED): a `>{\begin{math}}c<{\end{math}}` column type; the nmath environment in 2507.08909; adjacent pairs `$a$\begin{math}\end{math}$b$` and `\begin{math}c\end{math}\begin{math}d\end{math}`; captions and tables. A document with $ as catcode 12 received 0 edits. I did not trace why, so that is untested rather than shown safe.
refutation.attempts:
Read the producer at validators_l0_typo.ml:2644-2746 and the exemption scanner in validators_common.ml. Grepped all 2961 corpus papers: 13 files contain the trigger. Built the 10 candidate packages both ways, and 9 of them compile when unfixed. Wrote 12 minimal documents covering:
- lstnewenvironment, DefineVerbatimEnvironment, \Verb, \lstinline with braces, and \newenvironment{code}{\verbatim}{\endverbatim}
- filecontents* with \VerbatimInput
- an empty pair split by a % comment, and a spaced `\begin {math}`
- $ as catcode 12, and an array column type
- \begin{math} inside \mbox and \text, and adjacent empty or non-empty pairs
Four of them (\lstinline with braces, \newenvironment verbatim, the \mbox/\text case, and 2507.02165v1 from the corpus) do not compile even unfixed, so they were not judged. I confirmed the source edit behind each damaging case with LP_FIX_TRACE, and re-ran pdflatex by hand on the fixed source to get the exact error text.

INFERRED, not measured: hyperref bookmark text and custom listing environments made with newtcblisting behave the same way. Verdict: UNSAFE. The rule rewrites printed code in verbatim-like environments outside its fixed list, and its begin and end matching is asymmetric (spaced \begin, comment-split empty pair), which breaks the build.

MATH-106.what_the_fix_does: In math, rewrites \not= to \neq (control_word_repl adds a separating space before a following letter).
MATH-106.examples:
Real samples (5 papers, 38 pass-1 edits traced): all were plain '
ot=' -> '
eq', 0 hunks. MEASURED synthetic: 'a
ot=b', '
ot=\,', '
ot=_1', '
ot==z', '\mathrel{
